A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Energy Matching work. Their complete main texts, equations, tables, figures, and Appendices A–D are readable and support reliable comparison, including material moved between sections.

before.justification: v4 reports original image-generation FIDs, controlled inpainting, protein-design results, LID correlations, and sampling-time ablations.

after.justification: v5 retains original experimental results, revises ImageNet and MNIST outcomes, and adds original solver-sensitivity and computational-efficiency measurements.

M1.justification: Appendix D replaces the reported MNIST CNN–MLP architecture with a small UNet–Transformer, retaining approximately 2M parameters. Algorithm 3 adds optional data initialization and corrects the interaction-term sign/scaling to match the existing repulsion definition. The central scalar-potential model and OT-plus-contrastive objectives remain.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same two-dimensional demonstrations, CIFAR-10 and ImageNet32 generation, CelebA64 inpainting, AAV medium/hard protein design, and MNIST/CIFAR-10 LID estimation. The new computational analyses reuse CIFAR-10 without adding data or task coverage.

E2.justification: Appendix A.3 newly evaluates random matching against the retained LP-based coupling on CIFAR-10. Existing generation, protein, and LID comparator rosters remain unchanged. The new runtime table reuses DDPM++ and Tong et al.'s OT-CFM, labeled OT-FM there; these are not new baseline identities.

E3.justification: Appendix D substantially revises reported protocols: MNIST changes from 300k contrastive-only iterations to 50k warm-up plus 3.3k dual-objective iterations; ImageNet changes from 600k/5k to 640k/1k iterations and sampling time 1.5 to 2.5. CelebA budgets and schedules also change. The MNIST LID threshold changes from 10 to 3. New runtime evaluation specifies batch size 128 and 325 versus 1000 sampling steps.

E4.justification: New Appendices A.3–A.4 materially expand diagnostic evaluation through LP-versus-random solver sensitivity, OT training overhead, gradient-evaluation overhead, and wall-clock sampling efficiency. These address computational cost and solver dependence beyond the retained energy-landscape, sampling-time, and repulsion analyses.

E5.justification: The protein table retains the same standard-deviation reporting and values, moving from Table 4 to Table 5. No new experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are specified. The Gaussian standard deviation in A.3 is part of a mathematical argument, not experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Energy Matching's ImageNet FID changes from 7.67 to 6.64 in Table 2, and MNIST LID correlation from 0.895 to 0.877 in Table 3, alongside revised settings. A.3 adds random-matching FID 3.37. New Table 4 reports sampling times of 173s for Energy Matching, 136s for OT-FM, and 183s for DDPM++, with OT-FM FID 3.74 at 1000 steps. Most existing results and rankings remain unchanged.

T1.justification: Equation 4 corrects the JKO score term from rho_t to rho_(t+Delta t), with corresponding coupling orientation changes; Equation 3 removes the overlapping endpoint at t=1. Appendix A.3 adds a Gaussian distance-concentration derivation and solver-complexity discussion. The substantive LID derivation in Appendix C remains unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, contribution statement, and conclusion retain the same substantive claims: a time-independent scalar potential combines transport and EBM behavior, improves generation over compared EBMs, supports controlled generation, and enables Hessian-based LID estimation. Rewording and additional supporting analyses do not redefine these contributions.

C2.justification: A.3 newly explains solver insensitivity through distance concentration, while A.4 interprets fewer sampling steps as compensating for gradient overhead. Appendix D adds substantive guidance about equilibration, temperature switching, and low-dimensional exceptions. Existing memory and Hessian-computation limitations remain.

D1.justification: Section 2.1.3 newly distinguishes Euler–Maruyama training from Euler–Heun sampling and explains absorption of 1/epsilon_max into the contrastive weight. Appendix D adds SiLU recommendations, practical tuning guidance, fuller MNIST specifications, and the AAV Langevin count. Reported MNIST and AAV hardware changes to A100; code-access information remains unchanged.

R1.justification: v5 adds Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden on stochastic interpolants, Aggarwal et al. on distance concentration, and Ma et al. and Zhang et al. when positioning the method alongside inference-time scaling. Most other reference edits update bibliographic metadata rather than introduce different works.

P1.justification: v5 rewrites the abstract and selected methodological passages, simplifies notation and pseudocode, expands implementation explanations, and replaces some 'curl-free' terminology with 'irrotational.' Posterior-sampling material moves into the main text, Appendix B is condensed, and acknowledgments are added. The overall narrative structure remains recognizable.

P2.justification: v5 adds the sampling-efficiency Table 4 and renumbers the retained protein table as Table 5. Algorithm 3 moves from the appendix into Section 3.2, existing figures shift with the text, and architecture Figures 7–8 are compacted onto one page. Existing graphical evidence is retained.

improvement.justification: v5 resolves specific mathematical and pseudocode inconsistencies, clarifies numerical implementation, and adds useful solver and runtime evidence absent from v4. These improve reproducibility and support assessment of computational tradeoffs. The gains are limited: headline conclusions largely persist, revised scores use changed settings, and the ImageNet sampling-step inconsistency between Table 2 and Appendix D remains unresolved.
